claim: GDF15 is a member of the TGF-β cytokine family, also known as MIC-1 and NAG-1.
source: The cytokine, GDF15 (a member of the TGF-β cytokine family, also known as MIC-1 and NAG-1), is expressed in several tissues throughout the body and circulates in the bloodstream of healthy humans (Bootcov et al., 1997; Tsai et al., 2018; Patel et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Bootcov et al., 1997; Tsai et al., 2018; Patel et al., 2019).

claim: GDF15 is expressed in several tissues throughout the body and circulates in the bloodstream of healthy humans.
source: The cytokine, GDF15 (a member of the TGF-β cytokine family, also known as MIC-1 and NAG-1), is expressed in several tissues throughout the body and circulates in the bloodstream of healthy humans (Bootcov et al., 1997; Tsai et al., 2018; Patel et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Bootcov et al., 1997; Tsai et al., 2018; Patel et al., 2019).

claim: Plasma GDF15 levels increase dramatically in pathological states associated with cellular stress, including cancers, cardiac failure, chronic kidney disease, infection and obesity.
source: Plasma levels increase dramatically in a number of pathological states associated with cellular stress, including cancers, cardiac failure, chronic kidney disease, infection and obesity (Patel et al., 2019; Welsh et al., 2003; Kempf et al., 2007; Ho et al., 2013; Bauskin et al., 2006; Luan et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature (Patel et al., 2019; Welsh et al., 2003; Kempf et al., 2007; Ho et al., 2013; Bauskin et al., 2006; Luan et al., 2019).

claim: Over expression of GDF15 causes a dramatic reduction in food intake and weight loss.
source: Furthermore, over expression of GDF15 causes a dramatic reduction in food intake and weight loss (Tsai et al., 2018; Johnen et al., 2007; Macia et al., 2012; Chrysovergis et al., 2014; Xiong et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature (Tsai et al., 2018; Johnen et al., 2007; Macia et al., 2012; Chrysovergis et al., 2014; Xiong et al., 2017).

claim: GDF15 does not have a normal, physiological role but is secreted as an adaptive response to disease.
source: Together, this has led to the supposition that GDF15 does not have a normal, physiological role but is, instead, secreted as an adaptive response to disease (Patel et al., 2019; Luan et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Patel et al., 2019; Luan et al., 2019) and inference from the pattern of GDF15 expression in disease states.

claim: Transgenic knock out of GDF15 from the germline results in obesity.
source: This said, the transgenic knock out of GDF15 from the germline results in obesity, which could be interpreted that the cytokine has an alternative physiological function to regulate body weight (Tsai et al., 2013; Low et al., 2017; Tran et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Tsai et al., 2013; Low et al., 2017; Tran et al., 2018).

claim: GFRAL (GDNF-family receptor α-like) is the GDF15 receptor.
source: The GDF15 receptor, GFRAL (GDNF-family receptor α-like) is located exclusively in a small population of cells in the in the area postrema (AP) and nucleus of the tractus solitarius (NTS) of the mouse dorsomedial medulla oblongata, (Mullican et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2017; Emmerson et al., 2017; Hsu et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Mullican et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2017; Emmerson et al., 2017; Hsu et al., 2017).

claim: GFRAL is located exclusively in a small population of cells in the area postrema (AP) and nucleus of the tractus solitarius (NTS) of the mouse dorsomedial medulla oblongata.
source: The GDF15 receptor, GFRAL (GDNF-family receptor α-like) is located exclusively in a small population of cells in the in the area postrema (AP) and nucleus of the tractus solitarius (NTS) of the mouse dorsomedial medulla oblongata, (Mullican et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2017; Emmerson et al., 2017; Hsu et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Mullican et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2017; Emmerson et al., 2017; Hsu et al., 2017).

claim: The AP/NTS is a brainstem region containing neurons that have been linked with appetite regulation.
source: The GDF15 receptor, GFRAL (GDNF-family receptor α-like) is located exclusively in a small population of cells in the in the area postrema (AP) and nucleus of the tractus solitarius (NTS) of the mouse dorsomedial medulla oblongata, (Mullican et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2017; Emmerson et al., 2017; Hsu et al., 2017) a brainstem region containing a number of characterised neurons that previously have been linked with appetite regulation (Luckman, 1992; Rinaman et al., 1993; Larsen et al., 1997; Lawrence et al., 2000; Luckman and Lawrence, 2003; Ellacott et al., 2006; D'Agostino et al., 2016; Roman et al., 2016; Frikke-Schmidt et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Luckman, 1992; Rinaman et al., 1993; Larsen et al., 1997; Lawrence et al., 2000; Luckman and Lawrence, 2003; Ellacott et al., 2006; D'Agostino et al., 2016; Roman et al., 2016; Frikke-Schmidt et al., 2019).

claim: Administration of recombinant GDF15 reduces food intake in wild-type mice but not in GFRAL knock-out mice.
source: Administration of recombinant GDF15 reduces food intake, but not in GFRAL knock-out mice (Mullican et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2017; Emmerson et al., 2017; Hsu et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Mullican et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2017; Emmerson et al., 2017; Hsu et al., 2017).

claim: GDF15 induces the cellular activation marker, Fos protein, in GFRAL-positive cells in the AP/NTS.
source: It also induces the cellular activation marker, Fos protein, in GFRAL-positive cells in the AP/NTS, and in putative downstream targets in the pons and amygdala, (Xiong et al., 2017; Hsu et al., 2017; Frikke-Schmidt et al., 2019)
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Xiong et al., 2017; Hsu et al., 2017; Frikke-Schmidt et al., 2019).

claim: GDF15 induces Fos protein in putative downstream targets in the pons and amygdala.
source: It also induces the cellular activation marker, Fos protein, in GFRAL-positive cells in the AP/NTS, and in putative downstream targets in the pons and amygdala, (Xiong et al., 2017; Hsu et al., 2017; Frikke-Schmidt et al., 2019)
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Xiong et al., 2017; Hsu et al., 2017; Frikke-Schmidt et al., 2019).

claim: Selective surgical lesioning of the AP/NTS blocks the anorexic effects of GDF15.
source: whereas selective surgical lesioning of the AP/NTS blocks the anorexic effects of the peptide (Tsai et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Tsai et al., 2014).

claim: A small number of GFRAL-positive neurons contain immunoreactivity for tyrosine hydroxylase (TH).
source: Although a small number of GFRAL-positive neurons contain immunoreactivity for the catecholaminergic marker, tyrosine hydroxylase (TH), (Yang et al., 2017) relatively few TH-positive neurons are activated by exogenous GDF15 (Tsai et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Yang et al., 2017; Tsai et al., 2014).

claim: Relatively few TH-positive neurons are activated by exogenous GDF15.
source: Although a small number of GFRAL-positive neurons contain immunoreactivity for the catecholaminergic marker, tyrosine hydroxylase (TH), (Yang et al., 2017) relatively few TH-positive neurons are activated by exogenous GDF15 (Tsai et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Tsai et al., 2014).

claim: The highest proportion of GFRAL-positive neurons contain the neuropeptide transmitter, cholecystokinin (CCK).
source: We have extended these investigations and found that the highest proportion of GFRAL-positive neurons contain the neuropeptide transmitter, cholecystokinin (CCK).
evidence: Based on experimental data presented in the manuscript (immunohistochemistry and RNAScope).

claim: GFRAL cells are a sub-population of CCK neurons.
source: We demonstrate that GFRAL cells are a sub-population of CCK neurons, which respond to administration of GDF15 or the cancer therapeutic drug, cisplatin, but not to other anorectic signals.
evidence: Based on experimental data presented in the manuscript showing co-localization and activation patterns.

claim: GFRAL cells respond to administration of GDF15.
source: We demonstrate that GFRAL cells are a sub-population of CCK neurons, which respond to administration of GDF15 or the cancer therapeutic drug, cisplatin, but not to other anorectic signals.
evidence: Based on experimental data presented in the manuscript showing Fos activation.

claim: GFRAL cells respond to administration of cisplatin.
source: We demonstrate that GFRAL cells are a sub-population of CCK neurons, which respond to administration of GDF15 or the cancer therapeutic drug, cisplatin, but not to other anorectic signals.
evidence: Based on experimental data presented in the manuscript showing Fos activation after cisplatin treatment.

claim: GFRAL cells do not respond to other anorectic signals.
source: We demonstrate that GFRAL cells are a sub-population of CCK neurons, which respond to administration of GDF15 or the cancer therapeutic drug, cisplatin, but not to other anorectic signals.
evidence: Based on experimental data showing lack of Fos activation after fast-refeeding, lipid gavage, CCK, or LiCl.

claim: The effect of GDF15 to inhibit food intake is abrogated by the targeted deletion of CCK-containing neurons in the AP/NTS.
source: Additionally, the effect of GDF15 to inhibit food intake is abrogated by the targeted deletion of CCK-containing neurons in the AP/NTS or by pre-administration of a CCK receptor antagonist.
evidence: Based on experimental data using AAV-caspase to ablate CCK neurons.

claim: The effect of GDF15 to inhibit food intake is abrogated by pre-administration of a CCK receptor antagonist.
source: Additionally, the effect of GDF15 to inhibit food intake is abrogated by the targeted deletion of CCK-containing neurons in the AP/NTS or by pre-administration of a CCK receptor antagonist.
evidence: Based on experimental data using devazepide (CCK receptor antagonist).

claim: A single injection of GDF15 causes marked conditioned taste aversion.
source: A single injection of GDF15 causes marked conditioned taste and place aversions, suggesting a strong negative affect, as well as activating downstream pathways previously described as mediating anorexia.
evidence: Based on experimental data from conditioned taste aversion experiments.

claim: A single injection of GDF15 causes marked conditioned place aversion.
source: A single injection of GDF15 causes marked conditioned taste and place aversions, suggesting a strong negative affect, as well as activating downstream pathways previously described as mediating anorexia.
evidence: Based on experimental data from conditioned place aversion experiments.

claim: GDF15 causes a strong negative affect.
source: A single injection of GDF15 causes marked conditioned taste and place aversions, suggesting a strong negative affect, as well as activating downstream pathways previously described as mediating anorexia.
evidence: Inferred from the conditioned taste and place aversion data.

claim: GDF15 activates downstream pathways previously described as mediating anorexia.
source: A single injection of GDF15 causes marked conditioned taste and place aversions, suggesting a strong negative affect, as well as activating downstream pathways previously described as mediating anorexia.
evidence: Based on Fos activation data in PBN, PVH, CeA, and ovBNST.

claim: GDF15-induced anorexia can be blocked by neutralising the GFRAL receptor with a selective monoclonal antibody.
source: Lastly, since we can block GDF15- or cisplatin-induced anorexia by neutralising the GFRAL receptor with a selective monoclonal antibody, we suggest that the anorectic responses to disease and, potentially, their therapeutic treatment may be mediated by this distinct signalling pathway.
evidence: Based on experimental data using GFRAL monoclonal antibody.

claim: Cisplatin-induced anorexia can be blocked by neutralising the GFRAL receptor with a selective monoclonal antibody.
source: Lastly, since we can block GDF15- or cisplatin-induced anorexia by neutralising the GFRAL receptor with a selective monoclonal antibody, we suggest that the anorectic responses to disease and, potentially, their therapeutic treatment may be mediated by this distinct signalling pathway.
evidence: Based on experimental data using GFRAL monoclonal antibody.

claim: The anorectic responses to disease may be mediated by the GDF15/GFRAL signalling pathway.
source: Lastly, since we can block GDF15- or cisplatin-induced anorexia by neutralising the GFRAL receptor with a selective monoclonal antibody, we suggest that the anorectic responses to disease and, potentially, their therapeutic treatment may be mediated by this distinct signalling pathway.
evidence: Speculative conclusion based on experimental data.

claim: In the mouse, GFRAL was expressed in a continuous grouping of cells in the AP, extending into the medial region of the NTS.
source: In the mouse, GFRAL was expressed in a continuous grouping of cells in the AP, extending into the medial region of the NTS (Figure 1A), as noted previously by others (Mullican et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2017; Emmerson et al., 2017; Hsu et al., 2017).
evidence: Based on immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1A and supported by citations.

claim: There were similar numbers of GFRAL neurons in the AP and NTS (20 ± 1 per section in both).
source: Although dense within the AP and more sparsely distributed in the NTS, there were similar numbers of GFRAL neurons in the two structures (20 ± 1 per section in both the AP and the NTS).
evidence: Based on quantification of immunohistochemistry data.

claim: 60% of GFRAL-immunoreactive cells in the AP co-localised with CckCre::eYFP.
source: 60% of GFRAL-immunoreactive cells in the AP co-localised with CckCre::eYFP, though this proportion was 31% in the NTS (Figure 1B and summary in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Based on quantification of dual immunofluorescence shown in Figure 1B.

claim: 31% of GFRAL-immunoreactive cells in the NTS co-localised with CckCre::eYFP.
source: 60% of GFRAL-immunoreactive cells in the AP co-localised with CckCre::eYFP, though this proportion was 31% in the NTS (Figure 1B and summary in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Based on quantification of dual immunofluorescence shown in Figure 1B.

claim: RNAScope in situ hybridisation histology showed 69% overlap between GFRAL and CCK in the AP.
source: We confirmed this pattern using RNAScope in situ hybridisation histology, which provided slightly higher values of 69% and 35% overlap in the AP and NTS, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Based on RNAScope data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: RNAScope in situ hybridisation histology showed 35% overlap between GFRAL and CCK in the NTS.
source: We confirmed this pattern using RNAScope in situ hybridisation histology, which provided slightly higher values of 69% and 35% overlap in the AP and NTS, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Based on RNAScope data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The majority of GFRAL neurons are CCKergic.
source: Thus, overall, the majority of GFRAL neurons are CCKergic.
evidence: Inferred from the co-localization data showing 60% in AP and 31% in NTS.

claim: 27% of GFRAL neurons in the AP contain TH.
source: By comparison, dual immunohistochemistry revealed that 27% of GFRAL neurons in the AP and 45% in the NTS contained TH (Figure 1B).
evidence: Based on quantification of dual immunofluorescence shown in Figure 1B.

claim: 45% of GFRAL neurons in the NTS contain TH.
source: By comparison, dual immunohistochemistry revealed that 27% of GFRAL neurons in the AP and 45% in the NTS contained TH (Figure 1B).
evidence: Based on quantification of dual immunofluorescence shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Approximately 15% of GFRAL neurons contained both CCK and TH.
source: Overall, approximately, 15% of GFRAL neurons contained both CCK and TH (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Based on triple immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: At least 54% of GFRAL neurons in the AP co-localised with Slc17a6Cre::eYFP.
source: At least 54% GFRAL neurons in the AP co-localised with Slc17a6Cre::eYFP, which fits with the consensus that CCK neurons in this brain region are glutamatergic (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Based on dual immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: CCK neurons in the AP/NTS are glutamatergic.
source: At least 54% GFRAL neurons in the AP co-localised with Slc17a6Cre::eYFP, which fits with the consensus that CCK neurons in this brain region are glutamatergic (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Inferred from co-localization with VGlut2 (Slc17a6) and supported by established knowledge.

claim: GFRAL cells are distinct from NTS populations which contain PrRP.
source: Finally, GFRAL cells were distinct from other NTS populations which contain either PrRP or PPG (Figure 1B)
evidence: Based on lack of co-localization shown in Figure 1B.

claim: GFRAL cells are distinct from NTS populations which contain PPG.
source: Finally, GFRAL cells were distinct from other NTS populations which contain either PrRP or PPG (Figure 1B)
evidence: Based on lack of co-localization shown in Figure 1B.

claim: PrRP neurons form a separate sub-population of TH neurons.
source: Finally, GFRAL cells were distinct from other NTS populations which contain either PrRP or PPG (Figure 1B), which themselves either form a separate sub-population of TH neurons (Dodd and Luckman, 2013) or overlap with other CCK cells (Garfield et al., 2012; Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), respectively.
evidence: Supported by citation (Dodd and Luckman, 2013).

claim: PPG neurons overlap with other CCK cells.
source: Finally, GFRAL cells were distinct from other NTS populations which contain either PrRP or PPG (Figure 1B), which themselves either form a separate sub-population of TH neurons (Dodd and Luckman, 2013) or overlap with other CCK cells (Garfield et al., 2012; Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), respectively.
evidence: Supported by citation (Garfield et al., 2012) and data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: GFRAL cells form a distinct subset of CCK neurons, a proportion of which also contain TH.
source: In conclusion, GFRAL cells appear to form a distinct subset of CCK neurons, a proportion of which also contain TH.
evidence: Conclusion based on co-localization data presented in the manuscript.

claim: A single injection of GDF15 (2–8 nmol/kg, s.c.) at lights-out produced a significant and dose-dependent decrease in normal, night-time feeding within 2 hr of administration.
source: A single injection of GDF15 (2–8 nmol/kg, subcutaneous; s.c.) at lights-out produced a significant and dose-dependent decrease in normal, night-time feeding within 2 hr (hr) of administration (Figure 2A).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Cumulative food intake had mostly recovered by 24 hr after GDF15 administration.
source: Cumulative food intake had mostly recovered by 24 hr.
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Doses of 4–8 nmol/kg GDF15 were required to see a significant effect on fast-induced, day-time feeding.
source: Doses of 4–8 nmol/kg were required to see a significant effect on fast-induced, day-time feeding (Figure 2B), and were the doses used in later experiments.
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Administration of GDF15 supported a strong conditioned taste aversion when paired with sucrose.
source: Administration of GDF15 was associated with a negative affective valence, since a single injection supported a strong conditioned taste aversion (CTA) when paired with sucrose (see also Patel et al., 2019), and a conditioned place aversion (CPA) in mice (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 2C and supported by citation (Patel et al., 2019).

claim: Administration of GDF15 supported a conditioned place aversion in mice.
source: Administration of GDF15 was associated with a negative affective valence, since a single injection supported a strong conditioned taste aversion (CTA) when paired with sucrose (see also Patel et al., 2019), and a conditioned place aversion (CPA) in mice (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Administration of GDF15 to rats on 3 consecutive days induced pica behaviour to an extent comparable to that seen following injection of lithium chloride.
source: Administration of GDF15 to rats on 3 consecutive days induced pica behaviour – a proxy for sickness behaviour – to an extent comparable to that seen following injection of the nausea-inducing toxin, lithium chloride (LiCl; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Pica behaviour is a proxy for sickness behaviour in rodents.
source: In addition, pica behaviour, in which kaolin clay is consumed to remedy gastric malaise, was used as a measure of sickness given that rodents cannot vomit.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about rodent behavior.

claim: Rodents cannot vomit.
source: In addition, pica behaviour, in which kaolin clay is consumed to remedy gastric malaise, was used as a measure of sickness given that rodents cannot vomit.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about rodent physiology.

claim: GDF15 is probably not a natural satiety factor, but exerts a pathophysiological action to cause anorexia.
source: Together, these and recently published data (Borner et al., 2020a; Borner et al., 2020b) suggest that GDF15 is probably not a natural satiety factor, but exerts a pathophysiological action to cause anorexia.
evidence: Conclusion based on experimental data and supported by citations (Borner et al., 2020a; Borner et al., 2020b).

claim: Circulating GDF15 levels do not correlate with meal times in humans.
source: This conclusion is supported by the findings that circulating GDF15 levels do not correlate with meal times in humans, (Patel et al., 2019; Tsai et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citations (Patel et al., 2019; Tsai et al., 2015).

claim: GDF15 knock out in mice does not result in significant changes in normal chow intake.
source: and that GDF15 knock out in mice does not result in significant changes in normal chow intake (Tsai et al., 2013; Tran et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations (Tsai et al., 2013; Tran et al., 2018).

claim: A single, low-anorectic dose of GDF15 activated GFRAL+ve/CCK and TH neurons in the AP/NTS.
source: A single, low-anorectic dose of GDF15 activated GFRAL+ve/CCK and TH neurons in the AP/NTS, as well as GFRAL-ve neurons at the same level of both the AP and NTS (Figure 3A; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Based on Fos immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: GDF15 activated GFRAL-ve neurons in the AP and NTS.
source: A single, low-anorectic dose of GDF15 activated GFRAL+ve/CCK and TH neurons in the AP/NTS, as well as GFRAL-ve neurons at the same level of both the AP and NTS (Figure 3A; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Based on Fos immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: GDF15 does not significantly activate PrRP, PPG or POMC neurons.
source: Neither PrRP, PPG nor POMC neurons are activated significantly by GDF15 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Based on Fos immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: A group of GFRAL-ve cells in the medial NTS are activated by GDF15 but remain unidentified.
source: Thus, a very obvious group of GFRAL-ve cells in the medial NTS, that are activated by GDF15, remain unidentified (Figure 3A, arrow head).
evidence: Based on Fos immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: GFRAL cells are not activated by natural satiety signals acting after meal intake.
source: GFRAL cells are not activated by natural satiety signals acting after meal intake (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C); that is, following fast-induced re-feeding, the infusion of lipid directly into the stomach (300 µl Intralipid by gavage) or a low-dose of satiety-inducing, systemic CCK (6 μg/kg body weight, intraperitoneal; i.p.).
evidence: Based on Fos immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Only a small number of GFRAL cells are activated by LiCl.
source: Perhaps surprisingly, only a small number are activated by LiCl (128 mg/kg body weight, i.p.).
evidence: Based on Fos immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: CCK neurons in the AP/NTS respond to different anorectic stimuli and are probably a mixed population.
source: This contrasts with the general activation profile of CCK neurons in the AP/NTS, which respond to different anorectic stimuli and which underlines that they are probably a mixed population (D'Agostino et al., 2016; Roman et al., 2017).
evidence: Inferred from the differential activation patterns and supported by citations (D'Agostino et al., 2016; Roman et al., 2017).

claim: GDF15 administration caused significant increases in Fos staining in the lateral parabrachial nucleus (PBN).
source: In terms of potential downstream mediators of the GDF15 signal, in addition to the non-GFRAL cells in the NTS and AP, significant increases in Fos staining were recorded in the lateral parabrachial nucleus of the pons (PBN), the paraventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus (PVH), the oval sub-nucleus of the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis (ovBNST) and in the central nucleus of the amygdala (CeA; Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Based on Fos immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: GDF15 administration caused significant increases in Fos staining in the paraventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus (PVH).
source: In terms of potential downstream mediators of the GDF15 signal, in addition to the non-GFRAL cells in the NTS and AP, significant increases in Fos staining were recorded in the lateral parabrachial nucleus of the pons (PBN), the paraventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus (PVH), the oval sub-nucleus of the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis (ovBNST) and in the central nucleus of the amygdala (CeA; Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Based on Fos immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: GDF15 administration caused significant increases in Fos staining in the oval sub-nucleus of the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis (ovBNST).
source: In terms of potential downstream mediators of the GDF15 signal, in addition to the non-GFRAL cells in the NTS and AP, significant increases in Fos staining were recorded in the lateral parabrachial nucleus of the pons (PBN), the paraventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus (PVH), the oval sub-nucleus of the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis (ovBNST) and in the central nucleus of the amygdala (CeA; Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Based on Fos immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: GDF15 administration caused significant increases in Fos staining in the central nucleus of the amygdala (CeA).
source: In terms of potential downstream mediators of the GDF15 signal, in addition to the non-GFRAL cells in the NTS and AP, significant increases in Fos staining were recorded in the lateral parabrachial nucleus of the pons (PBN), the paraventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus (PVH), the oval sub-nucleus of the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis (ovBNST) and in the central nucleus of the amygdala (CeA; Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Based on Fos immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Some neurons in the PBN activated by GDF15 express calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP).
source: Using CalcaCre::eYFP or CrhCre::eYFP mice, we show that some neurons in the PBN activated by GDF15 express calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP), while many in the PVH, but not the CeA and ovBNST, express corticotrophin-releasing hormone (CRH; Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Based on Fos immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Many neurons in the PVH activated by GDF15 express corticotrophin-releasing hormone (CRH).
source: Using CalcaCre::eYFP or CrhCre::eYFP mice, we show that some neurons in the PBN activated by GDF15 express calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP), while many in the PVH, but not the CeA and ovBNST, express corticotrophin-releasing hormone (CRH; Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Based on Fos immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Neurons in the CeA and ovBNST activated by GDF15 do not express CRH.
source: Using CalcaCre::eYFP or CrhCre::eYFP mice, we show that some neurons in the PBN activated by GDF15 express calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP), while many in the PVH, but not the CeA and ovBNST, express corticotrophin-releasing hormone (CRH; Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Based on Fos immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: A large proportion of Fos-positive cells in the ovBNST and CeA contained PKC-δ immunoreactivity.
source: Instead, within the ovBNST and CeA, a large proportion of Fos-positive cells contained PKC-δ immunoreactivity (Figure 3B).
evidence: Based on Fos immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: CCK neurons in the NTS project directly to the PBN, including to cells containing CGRP.
source: CCKNTS neurons project directly to the PBN, including to cells containing CGRP (Roman et al., 2016; Roman et al., 2017);
evidence: Supported by citations (Roman et al., 2016; Roman et al., 2017).

claim: CCK1 receptors in the PBN have been proposed to modulate information flow from gut to brain.
source: and, CCK1 receptors in the PBN have been proposed to modulate information flow from gut to brain (Mercer and Beart, 2004; Saleh et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations (Mercer and Beart, 2004; Saleh et al., 1997).

claim: CGRP neurons in the PBN respond to a number of anorectic signals.
source: CGRPPBN neurons respond to a number of anorectic signals and may act as a point of convergence for different signalling pathways, themselves projecting forward to the CeA and elsewhere (Wu et al., 2012; Carter et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations (Wu et al., 2012; Carter et al., 2013).

claim: CGRP neurons in the PBN may act as a point of convergence for different signalling pathways.
source: CGRPPBN neurons respond to a number of anorectic signals and may act as a point of convergence for different signalling pathways, themselves projecting forward to the CeA and elsewhere (Wu et al., 2012; Carter et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations (Wu et al., 2012; Carter et al., 2013) and involves speculation about their role.

claim: CGRP neurons in the PBN project to the CeA.
source: CGRPPBN neurons respond to a number of anorectic signals and may act as a point of convergence for different signalling pathways, themselves projecting forward to the CeA and elsewhere (Wu et al., 2012; Carter et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations (Wu et al., 2012; Carter et al., 2013).

claim: CCK1 receptor mRNA is expressed in the lateral PBN.
source: Therefore, we used dual-fluorescence RNAScope to demonstrate the expression of Cckr1 in the lateral PBN, but found the receptor mRNA in relatively few CGRP (Calca mRNA-expressing) cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Based on RNAScope data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.

claim: CCK1 receptor mRNA is found in relatively few CGRP cells in the PBN.
source: Therefore, we used dual-fluorescence RNAScope to demonstrate the expression of Cckr1 in the lateral PBN, but found the receptor mRNA in relatively few CGRP (Calca mRNA-expressing) cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Based on RNAScope data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.

claim: CGRP neurons are unlikely to be the only target in the PBN for GFRAL neurons.
source: Thus, CGRP neurons are unlikely to be the only target in the PBN for GFRAL neurons.
evidence: Inferred from the finding that CCK1 receptors are in relatively few CGRP cells.

claim: Both GFRAL and CCK neurons activated by GDF15 project directly to the PBN.
source: By repeating our Fos experiment but in mice previously injected with the retrograde tracer, Fluoro-Gold, into the lateral PBN, we demonstrate that both GFRAL and CCK neurons activated by GDF15 project directly to the PBN (Figure 3C).
evidence: Based on retrograde tracing data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: CCK neurons in the NTS send direct projections to the PVH.
source: Likewise, CCKNTS neurons also send direct projections to the PVH (D'Agostino et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation (D'Agostino et al., 2016).

claim: Almost no GDF15-activated, GFRAL+ve or GFRAL-ve AP/NTS cells project directly to the PVH.
source: We confirmed this projection pattern using retrograde tracing, however, we showed that almost no GDF15-activated, GFRAL+ve or GFRAL-ve AP/NTS cells project directly to the PVH or to the ovBNST (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G and H).
evidence: Based on retrograde tracing data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G and H.

claim: Almost no GDF15-activated, GFRAL+ve or GFRAL-ve AP/NTS cells project directly to the ovBNST.
source: We confirmed this projection pattern using retrograde tracing, however, we showed that almost no GDF15-activated, GFRAL+ve or GFRAL-ve AP/NTS cells project directly to the PVH or to the ovBNST (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G and H).
evidence: Based on retrograde tracing data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G and H.

claim: GFRAL cells activated by GDF15 project directly to the PBN, which then activates downstream targets in the CeA, ovBNST and PVH.
source: The most parsimonious conclusion is that GFRAL cells activated by GDF15 project directly to the PBN, which then activates downstream targets in the CeA, ovBNST and PVH.
evidence: Inferred from the retrograde tracing and Fos activation data.

claim: GFRAL cells may synapse locally to activate other neuronal populations in the NTS.
source: GFRAL cells may also synapse locally to activate other neuronal populations, including cells in the medial NTS.
evidence: Speculative conclusion based on the observation of activated GFRAL-ve cells in the NTS.

claim: Injection of AAV-caspase into the AP/NTS of CckCre::eYFP mice caused an effective ablation of CCK neurons.
source: Post hoc examination confirmed that the designer caspase achieved an effective ablation of CCKAP/NTS neurons, assessed by immunostaining for eYFP and also GFRAL (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Based on immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: There was no significant difference in body weight between control and CCK-ablated mice over 10 weeks following viral injection.
source: Over the 10-week period following viral injection, there was no significant difference in body weight between groups (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Based on body weight data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mice with cell-specific ablation of CCK neurons in the AP/NTS showed an abrogated response to GDF15.
source: However, whereas mice transduced with control AAV-mCherry responded to GDF15 with a significant decrease in night-time food intake, those bearing cell-specific ablation of CCKAP/NTS neurons showed an abrogated response (Figure 4B).
evidence: Based on food intake data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Pre-treatment with the CCK receptor antagonist devazepide attenuated the anorectic response to GDF15.
source: We further injected GDF15 into mice which had been pre-treated with the CCK receptor antagonist, devazepide. Compared with mice receiving a vehicle control injection, those receiving devazepide displayed an attenuated anorectic response to a subsequent single injection of GDF15 (Figure 4C).
evidence: Based on food intake data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: At early time points, the anorectic effect of GDF15 was reduced by approximately half by devazepide.
source: At early time points, the anorectic effect of GDF15 was reduced by approximately half.
evidence: Based on food intake data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Cisplatin causes a long-term reduction in food intake.
source: Finally, the platinum-based therapeutic drug, cisplatin, causes a long-term reduction in food intake, which can have a major contribution to mortality in cancer patients treated with the drug (Dasari and Tchounwou, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation (Dasari and Tchounwou, 2014).

claim: Cisplatin-induced reduction in food intake can have a major contribution to mortality in cancer patients.
source: Finally, the platinum-based therapeutic drug, cisplatin, causes a long-term reduction in food intake, which can have a major contribution to mortality in cancer patients treated with the drug (Dasari and Tchounwou, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation (Dasari and Tchounwou, 2014).

claim: Cisplatin acts through the NTS → CGRP PBN axis in rats.
source: There is recent evidence that cisplatin acts through the NTS → CGRPPBN axis in both rats (Alhadeff et al., 2015; Alhadeff et al., 2017) and mice, (Hsu et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citations (Alhadeff et al., 2015; Alhadeff et al., 2017).

claim: Cisplatin acts through the NTS → CGRP PBN axis in mice.
source: There is recent evidence that cisplatin acts through the NTS → CGRPPBN axis in both rats (Alhadeff et al., 2015; Alhadeff et al., 2017) and mice, (Hsu et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citation (Hsu et al., 2017).

claim: A single injection of cisplatin (4 mg/kg, i.p.) led to a reduction in both food intake and body weight which lasted for three days.
source: In our hands, a single injection of cisplatin (4 mg/kg, i.p.) at the beginning of the dark phase, led to a reduction in both food intake and body weight which lasted for three days (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: Cisplatin injection led to a significant increase in circulating GDF15 which lasted for between 2 and 3 days.
source: In the same animals, there was a significant increase in circulating GDF15, which also lasted for between 2 and 3 days (Figure 5C).
evidence: Based on ELISA data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: After 1 day of cisplatin treatment, GDF15 levels were 45 pg/ml in vehicle-treated mice and 270 pg/ml in cisplatin-treated mice.
source: After 1 day, GDF15 levels were 45 pg/ml and 270 pg/ml in vehicle- and cisplatin-treated mice, respectively.
evidence: Based on ELISA data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Food intake and weight loss at 2 days after cisplatin correlated directly with the plasma level of GDF15.
source: Food intake and weight loss at 2 days correlated directly with the plasma level of GDF15 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Based on correlation analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Cisplatin activated GFRAL neurons in the AP/NTS, as assessed by Fos immunoreactivity.
source: In a separate experiment, we found also that cisplatin at the same dose activated GFRALAP/NTS neurons, as assessed by Fos immunoreactivity (Figure 5D).
evidence: Based on Fos immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Weight loss induced in rats by a long-lasting recombinant GDF15 protein can be blocked by a single, subcutaneous administration of a selective monoclonal antibody raised against GFRAL.
source: We have shown previously that weight loss induced in rats by a long-lasting recombinant GDF15 protein can be blocked by the single, subcutaneous administration of a selective monoclonal antibody raised against its receptor (GFRAL mAb) (Emmerson et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation (Emmerson et al., 2017).

claim: The reduction in food intake and body weight in mice caused by three daily doses of native GDF15 is blocked by pre-administration of 10 mg/kg of the GFRAL mAb.
source: Further, here we show that the reduction in food intake and body weight in mice, caused by three daily doses of native GDF15, is blocked by pre-administration of 10 mg/kg of the GFRAL mAb (Figure 5E and F).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 5E and F.

claim: 10 mg/kg of GFRAL mAb did not affect either food intake or body weight when injected alone.
source: Importantly, this high dose of GFRAL mAb which effectively blocks GDF15 signalling, did not affect either food intake or body weight when injected alone, signifying that GFRAL is unlikely to have a role in either satiety signalling or normal energy balance (for full mAb dose-response data see Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 5E, F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: GFRAL is unlikely to have a role in either satiety signalling or normal energy balance.
source: Importantly, this high dose of GFRAL mAb which effectively blocks GDF15 signalling, did not affect either food intake or body weight when injected alone, signifying that GFRAL is unlikely to have a role in either satiety signalling or normal energy balance (for full mAb dose-response data see Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Inferred from the lack of effect of GFRAL mAb alone on food intake and body weight.

claim: Pre-administration of the GFRAL mAb completely blocked the anorectic action of cisplatin.
source: However, pre-administration of the GFRAL mAb completely blocked the anorectic action of cisplatin (Figure 5G) and prevented the cisplatin-induced body weight loss (Figure 5H).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Pre-administration of the GFRAL mAb prevented the cisplatin-induced body weight loss.
source: However, pre-administration of the GFRAL mAb completely blocked the anorectic action of cisplatin (Figure 5G) and prevented the cisplatin-induced body weight loss (Figure 5H).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Increases in food intake in GDF15 and GFRAL knock-out mice are either sex specific or only clearly apparent in mice fed high-energy diet.
source: Thus, increases in food intake are either sex specific or only clearly apparent in mice fed high-energy diet.
evidence: Inference from examination of null animal phenotypes.

claim: One of the more obvious phenotypes of GDF15 and GFRAL knock-out mice is a significant reduction in overall locomotor activity.
source: However, one of the more obvious phenotypes is a significant reduction in overall locomotor activity, which might explain a major part of the obesity (Tsai et al., 2013; Tran et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations (Tsai et al., 2013; Tran et al., 2018).

claim: Reduced locomotor activity in GDF15 and GFRAL knock-out mice might explain a major part of the obesity.
source: However, one of the more obvious phenotypes is a significant reduction in overall locomotor activity, which might explain a major part of the obesity (Tsai et al., 2013; Tran et al., 2018).
evidence: Speculative inference based on the phenotype data.

claim: Hyperemesis gravidarum is associated with intense nausea and vomiting in early pregnancy.
source: In fact, the only non-chronic disease situation described, in which GDF15 is up regulated, is hyperemesis gravidarum associated with intense nausea and vomiting in early pregnancy (Fejzo et al., 2018; Petry et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations (Fejzo et al., 2018; Petry et al., 2018).

claim: GDF15 is up regulated in hyperemesis gravidarum.
source: In fact, the only non-chronic disease situation described, in which GDF15 is up regulated, is hyperemesis gravidarum associated with intense nausea and vomiting in early pregnancy (Fejzo et al., 2018; Petry et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations (Fejzo et al., 2018; Petry et al., 2018).

claim: Blocking endogenous GFRAL signalling with a selective monoclonal antibody does not affect baseline food intake or body weight.
source: This is strongly supported by our results that show that systemic administration of GDF15 causes robust conditioned taste aversion, conditioned place aversion and pica behaviour, and that blocking endogenous GFRAL signalling with a selective monoclonal antibody does not affect baseline food intake or body weight.
evidence: Based on experimental data showing no effect of GFRAL mAb alone.

claim: The AP and NTS are part of the dorsal vagal complex, which responds to gut-brain signalling.
source: The AP and NTS are also part of the dorsal vagal complex, which responds to gut-brain signalling.
evidence: Based on established neuroanatomical knowledge.

claim: GFRAL is not expressed in the gut or in the vagus nerve.
source: GFRAL is not expressed in the gut or in the vagus nerve, and since GDF15 is still effective at inducing anorexia in vagotomised rats, (Yang et al., 2017) the simplest conclusion is that circulating GDF15 acts directly on GFRAL expressed in the AP/NTS.
evidence: Supported by citation (Yang et al., 2017).

claim: GDF15 is still effective at inducing anorexia in vagotomised rats.
source: GFRAL is not expressed in the gut or in the vagus nerve, and since GDF15 is still effective at inducing anorexia in vagotomised rats, (Yang et al., 2017) the simplest conclusion is that circulating GDF15 acts directly on GFRAL expressed in the AP/NTS.
evidence: Supported by citation (Yang et al., 2017).

claim: Circulating GDF15 acts directly on GFRAL expressed in the AP/NTS.
source: GFRAL is not expressed in the gut or in the vagus nerve, and since GDF15 is still effective at inducing anorexia in vagotomised rats, (Yang et al., 2017) the simplest conclusion is that circulating GDF15 acts directly on GFRAL expressed in the AP/NTS.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of GFRAL expression in gut/vagus and effectiveness in vagotomised rats.

claim: Specific neuron types in the AP/NTS respond selectively to different sensory modalities (satiety versus nausea) to reduce food intake.
source: We and others have argued for the existence of specific neuron types in this region of the brainstem which respond selectively to different sensory modalities (for example satiety versus nausea) in order to reduce food intake (Luckman and Lawrence, 2003; Kreisler et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations (Luckman and Lawrence, 2003; Kreisler et al., 2014).

claim: The primary target for GDF15 is a distinct population of GFRAL/CCK neurons which span the AP/NTS.
source: Thus, we propose that the primary target for GDF15 is a distinct population of GFRAL/CCK neurons which span the AP/NTS to engage well-characterised circuitry involved in anorexia and conditioned aversion (Wu et al., 2012; Carter et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2018).
evidence: Based on experimental data and supported by citations (Wu et al., 2012; Carter et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2018).

claim: GFRAL/CCK neurons engage well-characterised circuitry involved in anorexia and conditioned aversion.
source: Thus, we propose that the primary target for GDF15 is a distinct population of GFRAL/CCK neurons which span the AP/NTS to engage well-characterised circuitry involved in anorexia and conditioned aversion (Wu et al., 2012; Carter et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations (Wu et al., 2012; Carter et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2018).

claim: CCK neurons activated by GDF15 project directly to the PBN.
source: We have found that CCK neurons activated by GDF15 project directly to the PBN, and that other downstream targets, in the PVH, CeA and ovBNST are also involved.
evidence: Based on retrograde tracing data.

claim: Downstream targets in the PVH, CeA and ovBNST are involved in GDF15 signaling.
source: We have found that CCK neurons activated by GDF15 project directly to the PBN, and that other downstream targets, in the PVH, CeA and ovBNST are also involved.
evidence: Based on Fos activation data.

claim: Anorectic signals utilise parallel downstream pathways with convergence at specific nodes.
source: There is ample evidence for anorectic signals to utilise parallel downstream pathways, but with convergence at specific nodes which we demonstrate are activated by GDF15, including CGRP neurons in the PBN (D'Agostino et al., 2016; Roman et al., 2016; Roman et al., 2017) and/or PKC-δ+ neurons in both the CeA and ovBNST (Cai et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations (D'Agostino et al., 2016; Roman et al., 2016; Roman et al., 2017; Cai et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2019).

claim: CGRP neurons in the PBN are a convergence node activated by GDF15.
source: There is ample evidence for anorectic signals to utilise parallel downstream pathways, but with convergence at specific nodes which we demonstrate are activated by GDF15, including CGRP neurons in the PBN (D'Agostino et al., 2016; Roman et al., 2016; Roman et al., 2017) and/or PKC-δ+ neurons in both the CeA and ovBNST (Cai et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: Based on experimental data and supported by citations (D'Agostino et al., 2016; Roman et al., 2016; Roman et al., 2017).

claim: PKC-δ+ neurons in the CeA and ovBNST are convergence nodes activated by GDF15.
source: There is ample evidence for anorectic signals to utilise parallel downstream pathways, but with convergence at specific nodes which we demonstrate are activated by GDF15, including CGRP neurons in the PBN (D'Agostino et al., 2016; Roman et al., 2016; Roman et al., 2017) and/or PKC-δ+ neurons in both the CeA and ovBNST (Cai et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: Based on experimental data and supported by citations (Cai et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2019).

claim: GFRAL neurons are not activated by LiCl.
source: There is still much to learn about these pathways, not least because we have shown that GFRAL neurons are not activated by the archetypal nausea-inducing agent LiCl, nor does GDF15 activate PPG (here) or GLP-1 receptor neurons (Welsh et al., 2003; Frikke-Schmidt et al., 2019), both capable of transmitting nauseous signals.
evidence: Based on experimental data showing lack of Fos activation.

claim: GDF15 does not activate PPG neurons.
source: There is still much to learn about these pathways, not least because we have shown that GFRAL neurons are not activated by the archetypal nausea-inducing agent LiCl, nor does GDF15 activate PPG (here) or GLP-1 receptor neurons (Welsh et al., 2003; Frikke-Schmidt et al., 2019), both capable of transmitting nauseous signals.
evidence: Based on experimental data showing lack of Fos activation.

claim: GDF15 does not activate GLP-1 receptor neurons.
source: There is still much to learn about these pathways, not least because we have shown that GFRAL neurons are not activated by the archetypal nausea-inducing agent LiCl, nor does GDF15 activate PPG (here) or GLP-1 receptor neurons (Welsh et al., 2003; Frikke-Schmidt et al., 2019), both capable of transmitting nauseous signals.
evidence: Supported by citations (Welsh et al., 2003; Frikke-Schmidt et al., 2019).

claim: PPG and GLP-1 receptor neurons are capable of transmitting nauseous signals.
source: There is still much to learn about these pathways, not least because we have shown that GFRAL neurons are not activated by the archetypal nausea-inducing agent LiCl, nor does GDF15 activate PPG (here) or GLP-1 receptor neurons (Welsh et al., 2003; Frikke-Schmidt et al., 2019), both capable of transmitting nauseous signals.
evidence: Supported by citations (Welsh et al., 2003; Frikke-Schmidt et al., 2019).

claim: Bacterial or viral infections are associated with secretion of GDF15.
source: Recently, bacterial or viral infections have been associated with secretion of GDF15 and an adaptive response in order to increase pathogen tolerance (Luan et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation (Luan et al., 2019).

claim: GDF15/GFRAL signalling increases triglyceride production by the liver to protect tissues dependent on triglycerides for fuel from metabolic damage due to inflammation.
source: In this ground-breaking paper, it was demonstrated that GDF15/GFRAL signalling increases triglyceride production by the liver in order to protect tissues, which are dependent on triglycerides for fuel, from metabolic damage due to inflammation.
evidence: Supported by reference to a paper (Luan et al., 2019).

claim: The loss of appetite and weight caused by metformin in diet-induced obese mice is dependent on GDF15/GFRAL signalling.
source: Also, the loss of appetite and weight caused by metformin in diet-induced obese mice is dependent on GDF15/GFRAL signalling, as is the accompanying increase in insulin sensitivity (Coll et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation (Coll et al., 2020).

claim: The increase in insulin sensitivity caused by metformin in diet-induced obese mice is dependent on GDF15/GFRAL signalling.
source: Also, the loss of appetite and weight caused by metformin in diet-induced obese mice is dependent on GDF15/GFRAL signalling, as is the accompanying increase in insulin sensitivity (Coll et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation (Coll et al., 2020).

claim: Increased GDF15 has been measured in the circulation of human cancer subjects.
source: It is interesting to note that increased GDF15 has been measured in the circulation of human cancer subjects (Welsh et al., 2003; Bauskin et al., 2006; Brown et al., 2003)
evidence: Supported by citations (Welsh et al., 2003; Bauskin et al., 2006; Brown et al., 2003).

claim: An NTS → CGRP PBN → CeA/ovBNST axis has been implicated in mediating the anorexia associated with cancer models in mice.
source: and, recently an NTS → CGRPPBN → CeA/ovBNST axis has been implicated in mediating the anorexia associated with cancer models in mice (Campos et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation (Campos et al., 2017).

claim: The NTS → CGRP PBN pathway appears to be activated by cisplatin in rats.
source: Likewise, work in rats has demonstrated that this pathway appears also to be activated by the platinum-based, cancer therapeutic drug, cisplatin (Alhadeff et al., 2015; Alhadeff et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations (Alhadeff et al., 2015; Alhadeff et al., 2017).

claim: Weight loss caused by cisplatin is reduced in GFRAL knock-out mice.
source: Although in neither case has the primary brainstem neuron been identified (Hsu et al., 2017), it is reported that weight loss caused by cisplatin is reduced in GFRAL knock-out mice, and we now show that this is true also if wild-type mice are pre-treated with a neutralising GFRAL antibody.
evidence: Supported by citation (Hsu et al., 2017).

claim: Weight loss caused by cisplatin is reduced if wild-type mice are pre-treated with a neutralising GFRAL antibody.
source: Although in neither case has the primary brainstem neuron been identified (Hsu et al., 2017), it is reported that weight loss caused by cisplatin is reduced in GFRAL knock-out mice, and we now show that this is true also if wild-type mice are pre-treated with a neutralising GFRAL antibody.
evidence: Based on experimental data showing GFRAL mAb blocks cisplatin effects.

claim: Both cancer and cisplatin treatment may exacerbate anorexia through the same brainstem pathway.
source: Although it is yet to be verified, the possibility exists that both a disease state (cancer) and the treatment (cisplatin) may exacerbate anorexia through the same brainstem pathway.
evidence: Speculative conclusion based on experimental data.

claim: GFRAL neutralising antibodies or antagonists may provide a possible co-treatment opportunity for patients suffering with cancer-related anorexia/cachexia.
source: If this is the case, then either GFRAL neutralising antibodies or GFRAL antagonists may provide a possible co-treatment opportunity for patients suffering with cancer-related anorexia/cachexia.
evidence: Speculative conclusion based on experimental data.

claim: The secretion of GDF15 during cancer is presumably an adaptive response.
source: The caveat to this is that the secretion of GDF15 during cancer, as it appears so for inflammatory infections, is presumably an adaptive response, so blocking GDF15/GFRAL signalling may worsen the disease and other symptoms.
evidence: Speculative inference based on the adaptive role of GDF15 in infections.

claim: Blocking GDF15/GFRAL signalling may worsen cancer and other symptoms.
source: The caveat to this is that the secretion of GDF15 during cancer, as it appears so for inflammatory infections, is presumably an adaptive response, so blocking GDF15/GFRAL signalling may worsen the disease and other symptoms.
evidence: Speculative concern based on the adaptive role of GDF15.

claim: GDF15 has been located in different tissues when they become cancerous.
source: GDF15 has been located in different tissues when they become cancerous (Welsh et al., 2003; Buckhaults et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations (Welsh et al., 2003; Buckhaults et al., 2003).

claim: It may be possible to bypass the systemic adaptive effects of GDF15 and selectively target the central pathways downstream of brainstem GFRAL.
source: If GDF15 has an adaptive systemic effect, then it may be possible to bypass this and, instead, selectively target the central pathways downstream of brainstem GFRAL.
evidence: Speculative suggestion for therapeutic strategy.
